utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. Today is Tuesday, the 26th of May, 2009. I would like to greet Mr. Praljak, Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Pusic, and Mr. Stojic. I would also like to greet the accused who are not present in the courtroom because they are ill. I would also like to greet the Defence counsel, Mr. Stringer and his entire team. Without forgetting the court reporter, the interpreters, the registrar, and the usher. We need to resume Mr. Praljak's testimony. I shall therefore give the floor to Mrs. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning to you. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General. We stopped at 3D001228, and we stopped at the part where it says: "Leave the trenches and repeaters and fill them in." So we will go through the document and also based on your recollection.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are the position that on the 17th of January in Gornji Vakuf were presented by Siljeg and Andric in the presence of Mr. Dzemal Merdan and Enver Hadzihasanovic, and they go on to say that the BH Army should assign a commander who would be subordinated to the HVO in terms of the chain of command and that a joint check-point be set up where Muslims and Croats would be represented proportionately. So that would be a mixed composition that the militant units, and this is primarily a reference to Paraga's units should withdraw to the villages, that there should be no troops with rifles in the town itself except for the military police patrols of mixed composition, and also to deny vile propaganda that the HVO had been killing civilians. And what happened was that they fired at an ambulance, and this is what was done by the BH Army, in fact; and that all of this in this area should have as its objective the establishment of peace. And this report which is signed by Enver Hadzihasanovic states that it is their opinion that this is an ultimatum and this is, of course, not an ultimatum. It's just a military position, a very clear military position. And in particular that the president of the SDA Abdulah 23 Topcic and Fahrudin Agic should have no influence over the army.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the last name of the person who are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I read the first paragraph of this document with a keen interest. Since it stems -- since it stems from the accused, it's all the more important in support of your case. Your overall theory is to say that the ABiH attacked and that it wasn't the HVO. So through your theory, I try to check this whether it was the Muslim forces that attacked, and I discover on reading paragraph 1 something which could be of interest. It seems that the HVO shelled a number of villages with artillery fire. The villages are mentioned. These are the villages of Voljevac -- I apologise for my pronunciation, and Pridvorci. Why did the HVO shell these villages? General Hadzihasanovic explains why, because they -- our troops had moved towards Crni Vrh. Therefore, military speaking, what happened where the ABiH moves, the HVO realises it, and then fires barrage shots and tries to shoot at the villages. What happened on the night of the 15th, does it really illustrate what happened and what occurred on the other side on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we will see in the document that follows a report by Mr. Andric quite specifically what this is all about, but here when it comes to Vakuf, we have already admitted documents from the Muslim side where clearly they write about what units they had brought in from outside to Vakuf from the direction of Konjic, through Here, from Bugojno, and partially from Central Bosnia. They wanted elements of the 7th Muslim Brigade to come in. Of course in such a situation where they in effect are preparing and you have seen from the document to take a broader region from the elevations that they had already taken in the town itself and around it that one has to -- a military response is required, especially so because it was always said withdraw the units that you had brought in from the outside. They're not needed here, and then we will withdraw too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise to my colleague. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. I would just like to bring to your attention that at line 24, at page 1, the -- I would just like to note that the number of this exhibit has been recorded wrongly. It's 3D1228.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On reading the first paragraph you could have done that but maybe you didn't see it and maybe your counsel didn't see it either. You could have, on the basis of the map, you could have shown us that the position of the ABiH at point 1303, that the trig point was such that the units were moving in a particular direction. You told us that a hundred people were working for you, so you could have identified those units that were placed on the trig point 1303. You could have discovered that there had been order and that they had been asked to move, and with your men you could have demonstrated that the HVO, having been informed of these movements had been given an order to fire barrage shots on the villages that are mentioned, and that is how you need to demonstrate things. You can't just make statements. That's not enough. You need to present compelling evidence in support of what you are saying, and generally speaking, these are documents of a military nature. Mrs. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would -- excuse me, please. I would add a question to the question asked by the President. According to what is stated in this first paragraph, one gets the impression that the allegation is that the HVO shelled with heavy artillery Muslim villages. Not positions of the ABiH but Muslim villages, and one then thinks that these are villages inhabited by civilians, and it is not easily -- it's not obvious that this was necessary in order to stop an approach of troops that had not yet reached these villages. Now, I wonder what your reaction is. I see that you have been shaking your head.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in all combat reports one should say, as it is often said, that units in such and such villages were targeted, but it's simply not done in that way. You say where the units are moving units are shelled, and then you say a village was shelled. It was not a village that was shelled. The reference here is the units that were advancing along that axis. The villages were not shelled because they could have been shelled earlier and so on. We're now talking about the movement of units, and then it is said like it is said in the reports by other armies, for instance, such and such town was shelled and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is why I said that earlier. If you had had orders from the HVO saying that since the HVO troops had moved in the direction of Crni Vrh, the HVO had to shell these two villages because in these two villages there were units of the rear, that then it would have been easy to establish a distinction between the civilian targets and the military targets, because as my colleague has said on reading this, one could believe that you knowingly targeted civilians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true, Your Honour, but if you take orders from any war, World War II and so on, they say, let's say among French units when they say such and such a village was shelled, the reference is to the army. What they mean is the troops were shelled. There are no villages around Crni Vrh. It's just the movement of the troops from Here towards Crni Vrh. And you have elevations listed here, Crni Vrh TT trig point, that's one thing. And another thing, you have a map here, Your Honours. I exhibited a map of Gornji Vakuf with the units of the BH Army clearly marked at every elevation. It has an IC number which, of course, I don't know at the moment, but it has been confirmed by the English major who testified here. And I didn't show it after that because I thought that it is very precise, and it has been confirmed by this English officer that this was the situation in Vakuf, the situation as I plotted it on the map. And I remember that I asked him: "Sir, to the best of your recollection, is this map accurate?" And he looked at the map, I remember quite clearly. He took three minutes to think, and he said, "Yes," and sign the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mrs. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: As far as the map is concerned it's 3D00464. That's a map of Gornji Vakuf, and I would just like to add something. We have admitted so far documents -- we have tendered into evidence documents that speak about the events in Gornji Vakuf until the 16th of January and even later on in -- into 1993, and I have to admit that we decided to use documents that have not yet been shown to the Chamber. The documents that are already exhibits, that have been admitted into evidence, were not used unless there was an important situation which they could assist us in explaining. Now, General I would like to ask you, Here, what is the importance of Here? What happened to Here -- what happened in Here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that. Later in 1993 an attack was launched from Here on Uzdol where some 40 people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And in 1992, after Prozor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Prozor, according to the documents that have already been exhibited here in this court, and the documents are quite clear because they are from the BH Army, plans were made to take Rama with direct attacks from Prozor onwards with clear tasks for everyone from Here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Where was the BH Army stationed apart from the town of Prozor? Do you know that? The BH Army units.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in all the villages with mixed population and in particular in the Muslim villages, and Here was one of major extremists attitudes, and units from -- the unit from that village did what happened in Uzdol, killed some 40 people. I was up there at the time, on that day, at that time, and we managed to repel the BH Army in a swift action, preventing an even greater massacre. And we managed to do another thing while we're on this topic. In the report from the international community, the European observers, there was no retaliation. I and other people who were there managed to prevent any form of reprisals except for the fact that I put under the guard, in accordance with the agreement, the local Muslim priest, and I put the guards in front of the mosque, and I now face accusations that I placed this man under house arrest. After such an event, this was the only way to prevent somebody who is really embittered and is perhaps might be tempted to commit a crime to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, you have the map in front of you. This line, Kute to Scipe to Here. Can you say is it relevant in the military sense?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said this is the road leading from Konjic both to Rama, so the eastern portion; and this road was used by units to go to the Gornji Vakuf area. They came from Bugojno. They came from Central Bosnia as we have seen from all the documents already exhibited. I cannot revert to all the documents now, not because I wouldn't like to do so, but if the Judges allow us another ten hours, this is what I want to do, because I want to be very precise and specific. And, Your Honours, I'm only -- I only have in mind the time that I have allotted to me, because I can use all these maps and show all these maps again, but I think this will suffice. I have already exhibited several maps here, was the Mujahedin camp. And while we are at the subject of that, in the spring of 1993, after returning from negotiations again to calm down the situation and at that time I was also in Central Bosnia, although Mr. Izetbegovic had not sent me a single Muslim to assist me in easing tensions, in calming the situation. So on this road, the negotiating team of the HVO with Mr. Andric, who was man number two in the HVO, at that time after General Petkovic were intercepted by the Mujahedin. They were looted. Their car was seized. They were stripped naked, and they were expelled to walk to Bugojno on foot in that condition. They were sent packing here at this spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you emphasise the Mujahedin and the Mujahedin camps. How many people were there all in all do you think, in this camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a mountain lodge, and I often passed by it, and I always stepped on the accelerator as I passed by it, frankly speaking, because you never knew who would be waiting there for you among these wild controllers of roads, but I could see them on the left side if you went along this direction, namely from the direction of Bugojno to this other direction. There were between 30, 40, or 50 people in this mountain lodge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there are 30, 40, or 50 of them. Maybe up to a hundred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot be precise. I really don't know. Up to 50, as far as I could see, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We know that you had artillery pieces. Was it that complicated? Was your artillery pieces, was it so difficult to shell them and then there would be no more camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. No, we did not have artillery at that point, that position. We were turned backwards. Actually, our pieces were trained to the position where the Army of the Republika Srpska was. It was not facing that direction, our artillery, and we wouldn't have achieved any major result to speak of, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you had mortars as well, not only that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is beyond the range of mortars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mrs. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, you referred to a report by Mr. Andric, and you said that he was in the Gornji Vakuf area. Please look at 3D03065. You're familiar with this document, and it was, in fact, submitted to you in 1993. Does the consent of the document reflect what you have been telling us in your testimony so far?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document is from my archives. It was submitted -- a copy of it was submitted to me by Mr. Andric, and that is a report that he had sent to Mr. Bruno Stojic, the head, and Bruno Stojic orally conveyed -- sent these five people for them to try and calm down the situation in the area of Gornji Vakuf, and that was on the 12th of January, 1993. And Stojic did so because -- probably because Petkovic was in Geneva, and a couple of days after they returned from Geneva, I'm not quite sure, and then they left for Geneva again. And I believe that they actually left on the 1st of January, 1993, and then stayed there up until the 13th or the 14th or thereabouts, and then they spent a couple of days. I believe Mate Boban in Hrvatska -- in Croatia, and Mr. Petkovic returned down there, and then they all again went to Geneva and stayed there until the end of the month. As for the report, it is completely correct, precise, and clear, and I have nothing to add to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course they say that the meetings were held on a daily basis. It wasn't the first meeting on the 17th. They had meetings every day from the 13th and on at the UNPROFOR base in Gornji Vakuf to try and find the solution. Of course, a solution that would not be such that it would mean that the HVO would have to be humiliated by the way in which they had occupied Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Please look at 3D02666.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document which comes from Colonel Andric, we can see that there were discussions between the HVO and the ABiH, but this meeting, in fact, had been organised because a soldier from UNPROFOR had been killed, and that was a problem that needed solving. One had to discover who had killed him and who put an end to the sniping. Was that not the main purpose of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, Your Honour Judge Antonetti. During a meeting, obviously, a soldier was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: On the first page?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the first page. So it was precisely for that meeting that Mr. Andric had been sent up there. And he says that the situation is tense, and that there existed a possibility of a major conflict erupting between the HVO and the ABiH. And then he goes on to say they got in touch. They agreed -- scheduled a meeting with representatives of the ABiH and when they arrived -- so the meeting had been scheduled for a completely different reason, but when they came in UN APCs, in the meantime they had learned that a UN officer had been killed and immediately proposed that the commission be set up to find out who had opened fire at him and killed him because when something like that happened, formidable propaganda campaign would be launched to accuse the HVO. Unfortunately, the HVO had a catastrophically low level of information capacity, and in that respect there was, in fact, an argument between Mr. Boban and myself, because in contrast to him I knew how important it was to inform -- to convey good information about the situation in the field. If something like that was done by the opposite side and everybody else and all the people in the international community who were representing specific policies of their countries, which unfortunately were not always in compliance, were not always in the service of calming down the conflict in Bosnia, then what would be aired would be a completely distorted and false picture. Therefore, whenever an incident of this kind happened - you remember the one in Mostar - the HVO pleaded and asked that there be set up a commission including UNPROFOR representatives to investigate the exact spot, the exact way, the positions of the respective forces from where the fire came so to conduct a proper investigation rather than just raise a din. You know, it was always the HVO, it was always some nebulous story about HVO sharp shooters shooting all over the place, left, right, and centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So let us now go to 3D02666. This is a power of attorney authorisation signed by Bruno Stojic and General Slobodan Praljak given to Jasmin Jaganjac. There is also associated with your joint actions aimed at relaxing the situation. Can you tell us a bit more about the circumstances when you gave this authorisation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jaganjac was also going to Zenica, to Central Bosnia, and up there, as far as I know, he also waited for Mr. Boras, a member of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And after that, you recall, there was an entire series of HZ HB and HVO delegations going around the terrain in order to try and calm down the situation and to have the Vance-Owen Plan that had been signed by Izetbegovic and Boban applied at least in respect of easing the situation, a cease-fire. And if something else was concluded at some new negotiations, the HVO was always prepared to always accept it, and it is so stated in every statement. That was what we were doing at that time, and that is why we gave this to Mr. Jaganjac. And we worked really hard and more than that, if I can say. That was the case with me and both Mr. Jaganjac in order to prevent an attack by the HBO [as interpreted] army, Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the HVO, to prevent a conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Looking at this order, I must say that I'm a bit surprised at this. A document was signed by yourself and by Mr. Stojic, and it was sent to all the military police units, including to the MUP and the commanders at the check-points. So we have the feeling that this order was communicated to everybody, including to three military policemen on the road carrying out the checks on the road. First of all, will they be getting this order? One may wonder. And secondly, Jasmin Jaganjac is probably unknown by all military policemen in the HVO. So was this order usable in military terms, or did they send orders simply for the sake of sending orders? Is this only paperwork?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was not only paperwork. It was an authorisation. Mr. Jaganjac had this paper on him at all times. First and foremost, Mr. Jaganjac was very well known in the HVO because he was the commander of Mostar in 1992. So his name was not unfamiliar. This was not an order. This was an authorisation. So he would come to a spot, and if he could see -- if there was any problem created for him, he would take out this piece of paper, and he would say, Here. Stojic and Praljak have authorised me, so-and-so, and it refers to all -- to whom it may concern, to whom I show this. Of course strictly speaking, strictly considering the right or -- or perhaps you could ask meet question: Who gave you the right, General, to sign this? Your Honour, law does not give me this possibility. It is not in the law. It is in the wish that I had for that man to be able to pass through various points and discharge the duty that the two of us were doing on behalf of Mr. Izetbegovic and in accordance with the agreement that we had reached, which was to work to establish peace. Secondly -- and the name meant something too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, we thought we understood - and at least that's what I understood so far - that you were officially the commander from July to November 1993. Here we have a document dated 26th of January, 1993 where the word "commander of the HVO --" the words "commander of the HVO" are mentioned. So how can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No explanation. I have no explanation, Your Honours. I'm not the commander, and had I read this up here when I was signing this, I would have crossed it out most certainly, but obviously it was typed the way it was typed. I know that General Petkovic was in Geneva at the time. Had he not been there, he would have signed it probably. It bears -- in the situation I signed it, so I have no explanation. But had I seen it, I did sign myself as a general, but I would never have signed myself as a -- as the commander of the Main Staff, because I certainly was not that, and I would have crossed it out. First and foremost, there was no commander at all of the Main Staff at that time. We had the head of the -- the chief of Main Staff. So it was just the speed of the action and the -- without me having properly seen what was at the top of the paper, the commander mainly, because I was not the commander at the time. The HVO at that time did not have a Main Staff commander, and that is my explanation and I have no other explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Would the usher -- no, that's fine. Let's move on to another document it is 3D00320, which is a book entitled "The Truth About Bosnia and Herzegovina," which has been handed round to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Have you received a copy of the book, General? Fine. Do Their Honours have the book in English? It looks like this. It's in the binder. It has a black title page.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now turn to page -- yes, I do need the usher's help, because there are two more binders for the Judges here. We didn't have time to hand them out.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Would you turn to page -- just a minute, let me find it. 3D in Croatian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter, the document we have is a B/C/S version. There is no English in this document. Will we get the English version?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is an English version. We couldn't fit it all into one binder, so the English version is in the hard cover binder. And I'd like to call up on e-court 3D12-0237, which in English is 3D28-0321 and 3D28-0322.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And, General, if you turn to page 100 -- or, rather, the document number is 100. Let me ask you about this book, "The Truth About Bosnia and Herzegovina." It was written by Mr. Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Miroslav Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Miroslav Tudjman worked on this book pursuant to my request, among other things. I requested that all the documents be collected which during the war were signed by any side. And it has to do, of course, with the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So any party, the international community, and everybody else. It was a very difficult job, because the documents were not put in the best order in the Croatian state at that time, and he went to a lot of effort to collect all these documents and to quote the sources. All I can tell the Judges is that we searched for the document on the recognition of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina by the Republic of Croatia. It took us months to find that document. So you see what the archives look like and the -- how the documents are stored. It took us a great deal of time and effort to compile this book, which shows us when the various peace agreements were signed, agreements on mutual relations, what time they were signed, where they were signed, what parties signed it, and so on and so forth. And that is why I said that this is a very important book if you want to understand the situation and the positions -- positions taken both by the Croatian state and also by the representatives of the Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say Mate Boban, Akmadzic, and all the others, the politicians, of course. And of course we have some military documents signed by General Petkovic and the like.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm waiting for the transcript. Now, would you look at document number 100, which is the Vance-Owen Plan, the agreement on future relations between the Croats and Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was signed in New York on the 3rd of March, 1993. In your testimony yesterday and last week, you mentioned the signing of these documents and the Vance-Owen Plan and the circumstances under which all this took place and how this was reflected on the ground, in the field.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on that particular day, the Vance-Owen Plan was signed by Mate Boban on behalf of the HZ HB; and the premier of BH, Mile Akmadzic; and on behalf of the Muslims, the president of the Presidency Izetbegovic; and the Foreign Minister, Haris Silajdzic, the Foreign Minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is. Now, of course we can't read through the whole text of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: It says that it was an informal agreement in the preamble. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, an informal agreement because -- well, it wasn't an informal agreement between the Muslims and Croats. It was informal because the third party, that is the Serbs, still had to sign it. So the agreement was comprehensive and all-embracing, but the Serbs hadn't signed it yet at this point in time, and so that's why it says "informal," in that sense; but the Croatian and Muslim side did sign it, and the joint side, because we have the Foreign Minister of BH and the prime minister of BH. And of course there was an agreement on the provisional order and system. Once again provisional or transitional period, because they were waiting to have the Serb side sign. So as far as I know at the time, the Croats and Muslims were supposed to work together to implement this agreement and then wait and see what the Serbs would decide, but that did not prevent the Muslims and Croats from implementing the agreement and what it stipulated as it was signed here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now turn to page -- or, rather, the next page, which is number 101, agreement, 101. The page in Croatian is 3D12-0238, and for the English it is 3D28-0323 and 3D28-0324. And this is an agreement on provisional organisation, Bosnia-Herzegovina, signed in New York on the 25th of March, 1993. You've already spoken about the different subjects incorporated into this agreement, but we are just showing this is an agreement on provisional organisation; and that it was signed between the Muslim and Croats. Do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The document speaks for itself. It's quite clear. So the two sides signed the document, and they were to work to implement what the document stipulates. And we wanted to provide the international community which had compiled this plan the possibility of exerting pressure on the Serbs more forcefully than they had been doing up until then, to prevail upon them to sign a plan of this kind, which was a good plan and could improve -- well, you could improve on it but generally it was good. And here the Croats and Muslims provided for the possibility of the great powers, the big powers, to -- the big powers to threaten Serbia or to lift the embargo and to use some other method to force the Serbs to sign up. Unfortunately, none of this happen. They did not exert pressure on them -- well, by bombing them, nor did they lift the embargo from us so that we could be strong and stand up to them and achieve better military results. When the Serbs saw that the international community was threatening with an empty gun, they refused to sign up to this, and so the Vance-Owen Plan fell through. And I think that some countries, as you were able to read -- well, America wasn't very much in favour of the Vance-Owen Plan. It had another plan. When they put the other plan on the table, the French and the English said, We doesn't like your plan. It's no good. And so while they were trying to settle the situation and see who was more important and would be able to wield more influence on the country, the situation deteriorated severely. And that's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A small technicality again. I think you have said that the agreement was of March 25. That's what's in the transcript. On the document it says 26th March, and I suppose 26th is right, but maybe you could clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see that. I'm looking at the Croatian text and it says New York, the 25th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And that is 100 and --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there's a problem with the translation there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Because 102, then, is 26.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 25th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the time difference. Perhaps the time difference explains it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is in the translation of the text. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look at this. It says withdraw of forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What are you referring to, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this document it says withdrawal of forces, of troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The agreement on provisional organisation you mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says the Croatian troops present in Sarajevo province will have to withdraw to the -- a province where the Croats were in the majority. So what is referred to is provinces with a majority Croatian population, not where the Muslims would expel the Croats or the Croats expel the Muslims. So as I say, the agreement speaks for itself. It's very clear and states everything that the HVO wanted to do beforehand, before the agreements of principle of Geneva which contained all these different elements.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: We can now move on to the statement under 102, which in Croatian is 3D12-0239, and for the English it is 3D28-0325 [as interpreted], and it is a report stating that Izetbegovic and Boban had signed the entire Vance-Owen Peace Plan in New York on the 25th of March, 1993. And this document repeats everything that you have already told us, but I would like to point out the last paragraph and the statement made by Cyrus Vance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter, since Ms. Kovacic, your assistant, sitting next to you can you just check that this is the right number, because otherwise I have to flick through the whole binder and look for the appropriate numbers, because here there is a mistake. It should not -- it doesn't read 3025 but 325, 3D --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 325. My mistake. I wasn't looking at the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But your colleagues can help you. Otherwise, the Judges will have to do your work.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The page number was 3D28-0325. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Izetbegovic and Boban signed the entire Vance-Owen Peace Plan, and what is important to note here is that the Serbs didn't sign. That's the first point. Secondly, that Vance expressed his regrets that the third party with Radovan Karadzic at its head decided not to sign the plan and go back home. So they refused to sign. And the third point, something that I've been saying, and that is that Mr. Izetbegovic says, "Now everything depends on the international community," because everybody expected the international community, within the frameworks of its peace solutions, would do at least something to force the Serbs to sign, and there were several options. They could either intervene, or they could enable the Muslims and Croats to have the embargo lifted so that we could be equal partners in the fight. And if they didn't want to involve themselves, at least not to have the Serb military supremacy prevail, that is to say to -- well, the Serbs didn't -- didn't take these international negotiations seriously. They saw nothing -- that nothing was happening except for verbal threats, whether they signed or not, just an expression of regrets, and a very benign diplomatic language was generally used but nothing actually happen. And I'm saying, Your Honours, that a situation of this kind then with the generals in the Bosnian army, gave rise to the thought -- they said, All right. Okay. We can't do anything to the Serbs. They're too strong, too powerful, but we're going to hit the HVO, and we'll reach the western borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then it's a fait accompli. The international community, without wishing to meddle into the conflict except in humanitarian terms, in giving humanitarian aid and verbally, diplomatically expressing their regrets and so on and so forth will recognise the situation on the ground according to the principle that those who had taken control of the territory can keep the territory, and that was the reason for --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the general kindly slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, Praljak, I was looking at the document while listening to you, and I was telling myself, and I repeat, and please correct me if I'm wrong, we discovered that on March 25, 1993, in New York you have the various participants to this famous Vance-Owen Plan. They went there to sign the plan, and one of them refused to sign, Mr. Karadzic, who refused to sign the plan. That created a lot of surprise. A meeting of this kind in New York with -- in the presence of all the media, where everybody is there to welcome peace was a real failure, because one of the participants refused to sign. As far as you know, were there any steps taken to see why Karadzic refused to sign? Did the United Nations Secretary-General go and see Karadzic and ask him, Why don't you want to sign? Has there been any actions taken by the diplomats to see -- to make him sign, because it was a complete failure. Have you studied is this point, or don't you have any answer to provide us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the next document which we're going to look at after this one, and in the transcript of the meeting of President Franjo Tudjman, Alija Izetbegovic, Silajdzic, Susak, Boban, and so on, you will see with absolute clarity what the positions were, what the line of thinking was, and what the positions were taken by these people. It will become crystal clear. You'll see what Franjo Tudjman thought. You'll see what Mr. Izetbegovic thought. You'll see what Silajdzic thought and what a tough time they were having, very tough to understand what the international community actually wanted. And I know that at that point in time the international community just introduced and enforced certain sanctions on Serbia, thinking that the Serbs would force -- it would force the Serbs and Milosevic to change his attitude towards the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina. However, the sanctions were violated along the Danube. Fuel was brought in that way, and I know how all this happened. So they had absolutely no relevant effect. They bore no fruit. They did not force the Serbs to sign something they didn't wish to sign for the simple reason that they had their weapons. They had their weapons factories. They had their stockpiles of weapons which would enable them to fight for another seven or eight years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Of course I don't want to discuss with you the sanctions, et cetera, but in some way I'm forced to say the following: That you mentioned that the sanctions had not been kept and they were violated, and you made a reference to the Danube, that fuel was brought in that way, et cetera. So it is in -- actually in line 16. Now, what I would only like to say that -- that I have been familiar with this issue. At that time there was a check-point at the Danube before the Serbian border, and -- and I know that a European mission as well, and Hungarian detachment which had to see to it that no violation be committed. But again I say that I cannot exclude some problems, but I just felt that I had to -- I have to mention this for your information. Thank you. 22 THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Prandler, thank you. I know 23 that there was a check-point in the direction of Hungary controlling the whole thing, but in the direction of Romania the situation was completely 25 different; and there was a pipeline transporting raw materials for some chemical industry from Romania into Serbia; and oil was pumped through that pipeline. But sanctions were violated, and you, yourself, Judge Prandler, you know that very well, that at that time the UN Secretary-General rejected any proposal by Morillon and by other generals from the international community to use force against the artillery of the VRS around Sarajevo and around Srebrenica and so on up until the very end of the war. Simply, militarily nobody wanted to get involved. They didn't even want to use the air force. And it is understandable to a certain extent, but it remains incomprehensible that at the same time the other two sides still had the embargo. It is true that it was possible to obtain weapons, but it was very difficult, and it resulted in a black market, trafficking, the destruction of the state authorities; and it cost four or five times more than it would have had it been possible to obtain it at market prices without an embargo in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to help the Judges understand, because what we've seen and heard is extremely complicated, according to you why did Mr. Karadzic not want to sign this document? What is your assessment of this? What is your take on it? Why did he not want to sign this plan? Do you have an explanation to give us or not? Of course you're not in his mind, but since you were one of the parties, you may have an idea.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, if you remember my explanation to General Quesnot. And yesterday, I read what they wanted. They wanted all the Serb lines to be united, and their plan for a Greater Serbia was still in place. They did not abandon it. It is a plan that was contrary to what has been said for years of what they wanted to achieve. They couldn't change their opinion, an opinion of this kind, or views of a conquering nature can only be changed if you defeat that party or if you make the other sides equal to have equality of arms and then they can defeat them. I am -- I was not in Karadzic's head, but I know his political views probably as well as he knows them himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as far as you were concerned, this plan did not coincide with the idea of Greater Serbia. That is what you're telling us, isn't?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. For your information, Your Honours, and regarding the question by His Honour Judge Antonetti, the question is at page 23, lines 23 and spilling over to 24, line 3, whether there was any response to Karadzic's behaviour -- or, rather, his refusal to sign, I would like to refer you to document P01924 [as interpreted], thanking my colleague Ms. Tomanovic, and that's the Resolution of the UN Security Council, dated the 17th of April, 1993, where -- which deals or, rather, which contains all the allegations that the general has just discussed and the answer to the question whether there was any response to Karadzic's refusal to sign. P is 01924. Thank you. We will go back to this book, but now I would like us to look at document P0173 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we are going to set aside the book soon, I went through it while you were talking. As you know, I work very fast, and I leafed through all the documents, and I realised something, and I would like you to confirm or deny this. In the constitutional and legal system of the Republic of Croatia, the president of the republic, in this particular case Mr. Tudjman does he have personal authority? Can he have international text adopted, and can he conduct international negotiations? Can as yet the head of the armed forces or does he depend -- is he entirely dependent on the Sabor, the Assembly, that can, if need be, issue an impeachment procedure if the president of the republic is not competent before the parliament? I'm putting this question to you, because I realised in the documents that you have provide us with that the deliberations of the Assembly of Croatia are mentioned on a number of issues, and I would like you to tell me whether the president of the Republic of Croatia has a degree of autonomy; or, like in any other parliamentary democracy, he can only act on the basis of a mandate that has entrusted to him by the Sabor or by his electorate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, at that time in Croatia, there was something that in political and legal terms is called the presidential system. So Dr. Franjo Tudjman had the right to pursue foreign policy and to control the army according to the powers vested in him as the president of the state. But within the constitution that was in force, not going outside of what is prescribed by -- prescribed by the constitution and under the control of the parliament. So all the decisions that pertain to some constitutional provisions such as, for instance, sending Croatian troops outside of its borders or changing the borders or any other major view he could negotiate or he could even sign something as part of the negotiations; but in order for this decision to be valid, he -- actually, the Croatian parliament had to ratify it by its vote. On some topics the required majority was the simple majority, and on some other major issues it was the two-thirds majority that was required to pass a bill. For those classical problems, all you needed was a simple majority of all the members of the parliament.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of your answer I can put a more sensitive question to you which is a key issue. The trial has been ongoing for three years now, and we really need to assess the essential element of this case. Now, if the theory of the Prosecution, i.e., as part of the criminal enterprise all the participants in the joint criminal enterprise including Mr. Tudjman and you, yourself, had there been any intention to annex Herzegovina, the Banovina, the Croatian territories that were part of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Should there have been a vote? Would the Croatian parliament have to adopt this before the Assembly for it to be ratified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Your Honour. Without two-thirds majority in the parliament after it has already gone through the parliamentary committees, nobody could implement such a decision, even if any such decisions existed in somebody's head. And I'm telling you, nobody had it in their heads. So the parliament of the republic, as the president -- as President Tudjman spoke, there's only God above the Croatian parliament. God, the Croatian parliament, and then everything else. The parliament is the supreme legislative and any other body in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question now. Then I'll give the floor back to your counsel. You told us earlier that you had asked Miroslav Tudjman to write this book. This book is, in fact, a compilation of a series of documents. Miroslav Tudjman is the son of his father, the late Franjo Tudjman. When you asked him to do this, did you say that he had all liberty to write this book, knowing that he was his father's son, or did you give him instructions, and did you tell him to refer to some documents and not to others? Or since he was an academic, and from what I understand, he was an academic; therefore, he is a free thinker, did he prepare this book as a free thinker and as any academic would do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, first of all, my Defence team has asked that ministry of foreign of affairs of the Republic of Croatia and of this office for the cooperation with the Tribunal the submission of all the documents that the parliament, the government, the president of the republic, the Foreign Minister, Mate Boban, all the documents that were signed and that pertain to these issues, and now please listen to me very closely. That's what I'm asking you. And if you ask us, we will submit those documents. After a month and a half, we receive a response, and they sent three documents. Three documents, Your Honours, of the documents. Three documents. After a week, we receive another letter, and they attach one more document. So a total of four documents out of 227 documents. And I am saying to you, and we have documents that -- memos where they manage to put together a grand total of four documents. That's one thing. And after that, I asked Miroslav Tudjman, whom I have known since the late 1960s because we studied together at the faculty of philosophy, we were not close friends but we knew each other, to gather everything, everything, and I mean everything. And this is everything, Your Honours. This is not a selection. This man is a scientist. He's really accurate and meticulous, and at the beginning of all those events he was not in his father's party. He was in the Liberal Party. So he's an independent man. So we're not talking about father and son. We're talking about my friend. He became a friend of mine during the war, and he is the person who collected all the documents. He did not make a selection. And there are no documents apart from these. And I have always said that without these, in my opinion it is impossible to understand this case and to, in effect, provide counter arguments to the Prosecution's allegation that the Croatian state, the government, the president, the parliament, and the HZ HB, Mate Boban, Akmadzic, and all the others, how they acted throughout this period. So that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Praljak. I think this calls for -- for some qualification. You say that this binder contains all the relevant documents. How come we have 20 other binders on our tables? What's in them, the same again, or are there other documents than these which are in this binder? Obviously it's not all the documents, so there must be criteria for selection. What were the criteria?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The signing of international agreements, Vance-Owen, Cutileiro, Stoltenberg, all the agreements at the level of state or national delegations, Izetbegovic signed it with Serbs, what was signed by Mate Boban, what was signed at all the conferences that were held to impose -- well, all the documents that are relevant for this topic. I didn't say relevant for the whole case. I'm just talking about the political and military and -- some -- with some military and so on. What was signed at what time and under what circumstances. Who signed first, and who tried to implement it; and why the Serbs did not sign; and why Mr. Izetbegovic then decided not to sign or renounce his signature, just the relevant documents on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: All right. I take that point of the limitation, but I still believe this is not all the documents. It's impossible, in my view. Because many of these documents I have now seen are press reports, press reports picked from certain - and I think Croatian - newspapers. The same events certainly generated press reports in innumerable newspapers worldwide with different emphasis, with different -- maybe also content, and they are not here. So a selection must have been made, but you are not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know. There is not a single newspaper article here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, Mr. Praljak. What we have been looking at, 102, for instance, that's a newspaper report from Vjesnik. I think Vjesnik is a Croatian newspaper. I may be wrong. And the previous one I do not know, but then the second one -- I think there are others. At least we have been pointed to one which clearly is. 115, again very much any list. Tell me I'm wrong, Vecernji List is not a newspaper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Vecernji List is a newspaper, but I've just said if the state does not have an orderly archives of the original documents, then what you have is not texts about the signed contract or signed agreement, but it is just a reproduction of what the journalists had about the signed agreement. I still claim that this is the original document which was published in the newspapers. This is not signed by the journalist as his work of authorship or his explanation of any event. This was in the newspapers or at the HINA agency, reproduced documents, copied documents in the form in which they arrived from the source at which they were signed. The journalist received a facsimile of the signed document and published it as such, and it was taken over as such. And it was taken over for the simple reason that the -- regrettably such documentation is not orderly in the Croatian government. So I claim that if anyone says that anything is wrong in respect of any item, I'd like that to be proven. I'd like anyone to show me that a letter has been subtracted or added to the original document the way it was produced and signed wherever, in New York or Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. There might be a linguistical problem in understanding the question of -- of His Honour, because when he asks about press reports, we understand it as a report prepared by a journalist, an original work of authorship by a journalist in the newspapers. In this situation, what we are talking about the following: The newspapers -- newspapers are a source, because all these agreements were indeed published in integral form in the newspapers. So General Praljak is trying to say that the agreements in question were published in full form in the newspapers, but these are not press reports. I just wanted to help explain the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I absolutely take that. I'm not saying that these are useless or anything but if you look, for instance, at 102, which we had before us all the time, there is a strange way that quotation marks are used. I must confess that I do not -- I do not see what the system is. But the -- the last paragraph, for instance, is written by a journalist. It has no quotation marks at all, and other newspapers may have said something else on this. I just want to draw back a bit the pretense that this is absolutely complete and there are no other sources in this field that might also be worth looking at. But I have made my -- my point, and you have answered, Mr. Praljak. I think we should not lose time on this now. It's not such an essential point after all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I realised that in line with what my colleague has just said, it's document which is not document 151 but 150, in fact. This would be a secret agreement on a -- about a confederation between Izetbegovic and Tudjman which had allegedly been signed in Geneva on the 14th of September, 1993. We have the text of the agreement. This text is interesting because it mentions this confederation, i.e., the union of the two republics, and this is in support of your arguments, but then I realised that in the footnote it says that the source of this document is the newspaper Vecernji List, 30th of June, 1994. It would have been useful to provide us with a photocopy of this newspaper article to understand how this came about. How was the -- was the journalist aware of the secret agreement? Was it a secret agreement between the participants? Did somebody want to convey this to the press? We don't have the answer to this question, whereas this agreement would have been of interest to us to shed some light on the theory of the union of the republic since we have seen a whole series of documents that had been entitled the union of the republics. You equate the document. You say that it comes from a newspaper, but we don't know what the origin of this is. We don't know how the newspaper got hold of it? Was it Mr. Tudjman? Was it Mr. Izetbegovic? Was it an anonymous source? Was it people who were close to these two men? We don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in September, around this date, you will see, and we prepared it precisely for the Court, Mr. Izetbegovic signed this secret agreement on a confederation between the Bosnian Muslim republic in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia. Over a couple of days -- in a couple of days in this same month, and you have the facsimile of the signed original documents there as well, Mr. Izetbegovic signed the document with the Serbian side which regulates Serb or Muslim relations. So this is a double play. We will show that. This could not have been published without the consent of President Franjo Tudjman, and the document was published in the newspapers as a facsimile with a signature of President Tudjman. Of course I can find the Vecernji List.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, you referred to one of the subsequent documents. I think it's document number 150, and I wonder whether we could get the page number of the English translation which I think would be at the bottom right-hand corner of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document I mentioned, which is number 150, is 3D28-0426.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I can give the original page number, which is 3D12-0290.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I just wish to add one thing in the meantime. We have not left this book forever. We have left it just in conjunction with -- with March 1993. We should be reverting to it again. And I shall also like to say I'm not sure whether it's in the transcript, that the secret of agreement on a confederation is in 3 -- in e-court under number 3D00451. It has signature. It has already been exhibited. So if it could be shown, I'd appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Namely it is only because of smaller number of pages. For the sake of that that Mr. Tudjman did not print all the facsimiles because it would have been a very thick volume. But all the documents were taken as facsimiles here, and here you can see the signatures 3D004 -- aha, it's here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, please do not overlap.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document from the 16th of September, signed on the 16th of September, would days later by Mr. Izetbegovic with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel and witness please not overlap. Counsel please repeat her last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 4D01040. Yes. And I made an oversight. I forgot the signatories because of the speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now have a 20 minutes' break since it's 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. First I should like to say that this document number 150 is a secret agreement on a confederation between the president of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Franjo Tudjman, and the president of the Presidency of the republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Izetbegovic has been exhibited as P05051 with Witness DZ. Likewise, this document under number 3D00298, from precisely this book, presented to the witness Zuzul on the 8th of May, 2008, on pages 27793, line 20 -- lines to -- 27794 up to line 15 Mr. Zuzul recognised the text of the document according to the allegations in the transcript, because he himself had participated in its production and signing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: As we have called up and referred to document 151, General, please look at page 3D12-0291. The English number is immediately following this, 1, 150. I do not have it with me at this moment, but this is a joint Serb or Muslim declaration of Alija Izetbegovic and Momcilo Krajisnik, Geneva, the 16th of September, 1993. We have seen this document already. It was also signed. Should you like to give us any additional information about that document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So two days after Mr. Izetbegovic had agreed with Mr. Franjo Tudjman, the president of the Republic of Croatia that they would work to establish a joint state of Croats and Muslims in the union of Bosnia and Herzegovina but simultaneously thus established state would be part of confederal structure with the Republic of Croatia, and that is the foundation of what is referred to as the Washington Accords, the Washington Agreement from 1994 which actually was created on that basis. And the -- A federation and, B, confederation with Croatia. Later regrettably the idea of the confederation was abandoned as if it had never existed and the federation got 51 percent of the territory. In this second document, number 151, what is of importance is item 1. All items are important, of course, but this is the one that is mostly important, which is that immediate cessation of all hostilities and military conflicts was agreed between the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the army of the Bosnian Serbs. And the military agreement was signed. Some lines were established between their commanders, and thereby the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina unilaterally stopped fighting with the -- at that time, Army of the Republika Srpska, and that is the period. That is the time when Sefer Halilovic and Rasim Delic initiated the last part of the offensives against the Croats in the Neretva River valley from Uskoplje, and that is the time of the fiercest attacks over an area of 200 kilometres from Vakuf to Mostar. And item 5, they agreed on disengagement between Serbs and Muslims, demarcation between Serbs and Muslims, a territory on demarcation of the three republics that would form the union of which two republics, the Croatian and the Muslim ones, would enter into a confederation with Croatia. They say that a referendum needs to be prepared, but they also say that they will ask the citizens whether they wish to remain in a union or wish to leave it. So Bosnia and Herzegovina you can see with the signatures of Izetbegovic and Krajisnik and Stoltenberg and Owen is divided. Citizens are being given the right to say, We don't want to live in it; and we know what the Serbs decision would be. And it also says that in the case of a dissolution of the union, all the rights are vested in the union or the rights of the union of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including membership of the United Nations shall be automatically transferred to the republic with the predominantly Muslim population. So as the part that was occupied by Serbia had been more or less -- by Serbs had been more or less ethnically cleansed, what remained in this federation of Muslims and Croats was, of course, already predominantly Muslim populated, and that is what they called it. And so they say, Okay, When we part ways, if that is shown by the referendum results, we shall remain members of the United Nations, et cetera. So who is dividing Bosnia and Herzegovina? Here you can see who is dividing Bosnia and Herzegovina. There you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. This joint Serbian-Muslim declaration is number 3D00451, Exhibit -- it's already an exhibit and admitted by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just mention that they are discussing an outlet to the sea and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: We're now going to leave the book for the time being, but we will come back to it in due course. And now would you look at document P01739, please. We have prepared a copy for Their Honours and for Mr. Stringer for them on it able to follow more easily. It is the record or minutes from a meeting held in the office of the president of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman. Are you aware of this record, and do you know of its contents?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Franjo Tudjman, Alija Izetbegovic, Haris Silajdzic, Gojko Susak. I think Minister Jarnjak was there, too, the minister of the interior of the republic of Croatia, that is, Ivan Jarnjak. And another ambassador, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Was it Mr. Sancevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was Sancevic. Let me have a look. Well, they were the main people, Sancevic is by the by.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Since you've looked at the document, could you tell us the topics discussed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the topics that were discussed were in a way very broad, but they had to do with the problem of the conflict between the HVO and the BH Army, and Mr. Izetbegovic -- the president says it's a problem. That's the main problem. How to prevent those clashes and conflicts, and Mr. Izetbegovic says we'll send some people over there. He failed to send anybody, and then he goes on to say that are anybody from the BH Army who would obstruct the agreement would be dismissed, but he says he doesn't know the facts he doesn't know who is obstructing the process. He didn't who was doing what. He didn't know how the conflicts and clashes came about, and he goes on to say that it is something that should not happen but there are always mad men on all sides, and they don't live in the logical realistic world, the realm of logic. Then he goes on to discuss another matter, and we have a series of speeches here. Well, the Serbs didn't sign. The Serbs failed to sign the agreement and now, over all these pages, they are debating who -- which international forces are standing behind the Serbs. So Tudjman, Izetbegovic, Silajdzic, Susak are trying to understand the situation, to understand why the international community doesn't have more influence and isn't exerting more pressure on the Serbs. Izetbegovic is fully conscious of the fact that they won't sign ultimately, and then it's clear to them that in the Pentagon there is resistance toward any kind of intervention. And then they're trying to see who said what from amongst the international community and what it is that the international community wants at all in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And so that is what is contained in this record and these pages, and you should read them carefully, first of all to see that these people know that they themselves alone cannot solve the problem, that they have to keep reading what the individual countries of the West, England, France, America think and what their intentions and interests are for them then to be able to adapt themselves to those interests. And then they're discussing whether the sanctions against Serbia are going to bear fruit, are going to have any influence, and they hope that they will. Then they come to realise that they probably won't have much influence and that Mladic is leading the army in the way he sees fit, and that the question is whether he's listening to Karadzic and Milosevic at all any more and so on. Then President Tudjman goes on to ask why the West allowed Serbia in the first place to carry out an aggression and why those people in the internal negotiations with him raise the question of the possible survival of Bosnia-Herzegovina at all. And then they're not quite sure whether the West wants to create Republika Srpska which it did create in the way it created it ultimately. And from this it follows and one can see that Tudjman says, "Okay. Let's -- let's resort to plan B. If the international community through its force and strength decides to create Republika Srpska, let's resort to plan B, the Croats and Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Let's create a joint front." And he says that quite explicitly. And mention is made of Christopher Bartholomew and so on. It's a very important document for us to be able to see --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, I apologise for interrupting you, but the document and meeting was held on the 27th of March, 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Immediately after the events -- or, rather, the signing of the agreement that we previously saw of the 3rd of March and the 25th of March. So we're now talking about what happened in New York; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They came back. They signed an agreement but without the Serbs, and now they saw that nobody was going to force the Serbs to sign. They're trying to see why all this is happening in Yugoslavia since the 1990s, why the situation has developed in the way it has. Of course, there's something afoot, and the president says that they now have to decide, page 01322408 in Croatian, he says that, "We should decide what the Croatian and Muslim policy should be," that they should try and be realistic and preserve the maximum possible when facing with the situation we're facing. So this is a classical sentence uttered by President Tudjman. The world as it is. He kept repeating this phrase, such and such a world. The world we live in is reality, the fact that they are waging a policy isn't a policy of principle, but it is a forceful strong policy which has the strength to implement whether -- to implement what was publicly agreed or agreed behind the scenes. And he says that one faced with the world of this kind, with the world as it is, we cannot do anything but see what we can do to gain the maximum for us in a world of that kind, as it is. And then Silajdzic goes on to say what Owen promised Karadzic and so on. Mr. Izetbegovic says he understands that they're going to exert pressure on the weakest -- on the weaker side, and if Karadzic fails to agree then the international community will say, right, Karadzic has not agreed and you see the borders so that he can be satisfied, because as far as they were concerned, peace was the most essential point. Now, what form this peace would take and who would suffer under that kind of peace and who would lose what and what happened to the principles of that peace all that was left out in the open and as far as international policy in the Balkans was concerned, from the annexing of Bosnia and Herzegovina by Austria in 1878, Austria's election and so on, nobody cared, nobody could care less. Nobody waged a policy of principle at all, but it was just a policy of interest that was waged. And then Izetbegovic goes on to say that Owen had, in fact, stated that there would be no Serb republic. And as we know full well, they were given a Serb republic. They obtained it, and so on and so forth. And, of course, at one point, President Tudjman says that if that happens, we would resort to what they had agreed upon, to form a joint Croatian and Muslim state in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We'll go together.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that page number is, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find it just now, but let's look at what's important on that page, 01322415. On that page, Silajdzic says that President Mitterrand had somewhat changed his opinion vis-à-vis the support he lent to the Serbs at the beginning. So France at this point was more prone to enforce a logical solution, but the English weren't in favour of that. Then you had the problem of Russians and all this combined, and President Tudjman says again two pages later that one must be very resolute and united and simply not allow them to implement their policy. Silajdzic then goes on to say that the West expects Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina to cooperate closely because they would thereby facilitate matters and their pressure exerted on the Serbs, and that was in a way conditional to this. So it's a complicated piece of writing but which speaks volumes about the facts that are relevant for an understanding of the relationships between the Muslims and Croats and the international community and how weak the leadership was, in fact, both in Bosnia-Herzegovina and of Croatia, weak to do anything against the will of the international community. And mention is made of the fact that Croatia is helping to arm Bosnia-Herzegovina. The embargo is mentioned. They say the Americans had promised to lift the embargo on certain weapons, but nothing came of that, of course. And then Izetbegovic, on one of the pages, says that Buha had told him that they wanted to take control of Eastern Bosnia and that Eastern Bosnia was Serbian and that there was no question of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Who was Buha?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the Foreign Minister of Republika Srpska and that he would expel the Muslims from there, which they which they, in fact, did with the genocide in Srebrenica except for Gorazde. Now, Mr. Izetbegovic was conscious of the fact that the Serbs could defeat the BH Army in Eastern Bosnia, for instance. And this happened, with the exception of Gorazde, as I've already said, that they would not manage to take control of Sarajevo. So that's it roughly, right up until the time when they mention names, when they name names.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, this was after your talks about -- your discussions about the events in Konjic and the shipment of weapons; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 01322421 is the page number in the Croatian version where Mr. Izetbegovic, on the previous page, first refers to Srebrenica and says that the situation is very difficult over there. He speaks about some 400 metres that they managed to advance and so on, and that the problem was survival there and not whether the Serbs would take control of the town or not; but that it was pure survival and the people over there would fight to the very end, of course with the help and assistance once again of what later happened, that is that it was protected area the people gave up their arms and then what happened happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Tuzla is mentioned too?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Tuzla is mentioned. And Mr. Izetbegovic says that he would travel to Tuzla, and then I think Susak intervened because Susak had had enough, because there was a BH Army attack in Konjic on the HVO, and he says let's solve Konjic first, and then Mr. Izetbegovic says, "But we'll solve the situation in Konjic, of course." And that's a classical phrase of his, we'll resolve it, we'll solve it. He doesn't say I'll go to Konjic. I'll send my best men there, but he says assumes it will be resolved in one way or another, that the appointed leader of Konjic, Jablanica, and Rama would deal with the matter. Cibo, that Cibo would deal with it according to perhaps a secret agreement. Anyway Gojko Susak says well he's quite nervous there, and he reacts quite roughly, and he says, Alija you got five planes in Zagreb. Three are on their way, and he says, I'm not going to provide the BH Army with any more weapons so that they can use those weapons expel the Croats and attack the HVO, and that's the terrible problem that I spoke to you about earlier on. And then he mentions a man called Praljak, who's sitting here before you, and he says that Praljak is not an unreasonable man, and I agree with that, and that he's pissing blood down there with Jaganjac day and night to try and deal with the situation. Of course I wasn't alone. Petkovic did that too and so did Stojic and all the rest of them. So they went and toured all those Konjic places and wherever and tried to reach some agreement. And Susak is recounting what happened and says that I was very angry, but I wasn't in a panic. The word "panic" does not -- cannot be attached to me. I'm never in a panic. I can be angry or bitter because they were tricking us, but not in a panic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Did you expect to come into contact with President Izetbegovic and to see him upon his return from New York?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Either him or in any other way.
